title: The Small Conjecture
statement_text: Every small hereditary class has bounded twin-width.
context_text: Twin-width is defined through contraction sequences: starting from $G$, repeatedly merge two vertices into one, keeping black edges to common neighbours and turning into red edges the adjacencies that are inconsistent (to vertices adjacent to only one of them, or already red); $G$ has twin-width at most $d$ if it can be reduced to a single vertex while every intermediate trigraph has red degree at most $d$. A class has bounded twin-width if all its graphs have twin-width at most some $d$. A class is small if there is a constant $c$ such that it contains at most $n!\,c^n$ graphs on the vertex set $[n]$, for every $n$; it is hereditary if closed under induced subgraphs. The authors prove that every class of bounded twin-width is small, unifying the facts that bounded treewidth classes, proper subclasses of permutation graphs (Marcus–Tardos) and proper minor-closed classes (Norine et al.) are small, and provocatively conjecture the converse for hereditary classes. As evidence they show that seemingly complex small hereditary classes have bounded twin-width: the $s$-subdivisions of $K_n$ have bounded twin-width if and only if $s=\Omega(\log n)$, graphs of bounded stack or queue number, and some cubic expanders (from iterated random $2$-lifts), whereas non-small classes such as interval graphs, subcubic graphs or random cubic graphs do not. A prerequisite is bounded symmetric difference (every graph has two vertices whose neighbourhoods differ on at most $d$ vertices), and even showing that small hereditary classes have this property is unclear; a very particular case is that every small hereditary class with no $K_{2,2}$ subgraph has bounded minimum degree. They also note a possible connection with group theory via Cayley graphs. Status note (November 2026): refuted by Bonnet, Geniet, Tessera and Thomassé ('Twin-width VII: groups', arXiv 2204.12330, 2022), as also noted in the final version of Twin-width I (arXiv 2004.14789).

title: Implicit Graph Conjecture
statement_text: Every factorial hereditary class (i.e., hereditary class with growth $n!^{O(1)}$) admits an $O(\log n)$-adjacency labeling scheme.
context_text: The implicit graph conjecture posits that any hereditary graph class with at most $n!^{O(1)}$ labeled $n$-vertex graphs has an adjacency labeling scheme using $O(\log n)$ bits per vertex. The paper obtains such a scheme for all bounded twin-width classes as a second consequence of the linear-arity contraction tree, confirming the conjecture for this broad family.
paper_contribution: Proves that every graph class of bounded twin-width admits an $O(\log n)$-adjacency labeling scheme, confirming the implicit graph conjecture for all bounded twin-width hereditary classes.

title: Question: polynomial expansion and twin-width
statement_text: Do classes with polynomial expansion have bounded twin-width?
context_text: Twin-width is defined through contraction sequences: starting from $G$, repeatedly merge two vertices into one, keeping black edges to common neighbours and turning into red edges the adjacencies that are inconsistent (to vertices adjacent to only one of them, or already red); $G$ has twin-width at most $d$ if it can be reduced to a single vertex while every intermediate trigraph has red degree at most $d$. A class has bounded twin-width if all its graphs have twin-width at most some $d$. A class is small if there is a constant $c$ such that it contains at most $n!\,c^n$ graphs on the vertex set $[n]$, for every $n$; it is hereditary if closed under induced subgraphs. For $r\ge0$, an $r$-shallow minor of $G$ is a minor whose branch sets induce subgraphs of radius at most $r$; $\nabla_r(G)$ is the maximum of $|E(H)|/|V(H)|$ over $r$-shallow minors $H$ of $G$, and a class has expansion $f$ if $\nabla_r(G)\le f(r)$ for all its graphs and all $r$; it has polynomial expansion if $f$ can be taken polynomial (proper minor-closed classes even have constant expansion). Dvořák and Norine showed that classes with expansion $r\mapsto c^{r^{1/3-\varepsilon}}$ are small, so classes with polynomial expansion are small, and the small conjecture of the authors (every small hereditary class has bounded twin-width) would imply that they have bounded twin-width. The authors propose, as a first but challenging step towards the small conjecture, to show that small sparse classes have bounded (sparse) twin-width, this question being a particular instance. The authors show that five natural ways of restricting twin-width to sparse classes coincide (bounded sparse twin-width), e.g. hereditary classes of bounded twin-width excluding some $K_{t,t}$ subgraph, or whose graphs have linearly many edges. The converse inclusion fails: the authors construct cubic expanders of bounded twin-width, so bounded sparse twin-width classes do not necessarily have polynomial expansion.
